```{r}

#| include: false

Sys.setenv(TZ = "UTC")

knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5)

                                    "../../dev/article-data/plot-sampling"))
knitr::read_chunk(file.path(data_dir, "simulate_population.R"))
```

This article constructs a simulated forest population for the plot-sampling
examples. We use real forest boundaries and plot locations from Weisse Krug
in Germany, together with canopy-height measurements derived from UAV-based
LiDAR [@spitta2026lidar].[^uav-data] We simulate tree counts for three species and five
diameter classes using the magnitude-composition model [@finley2026magcompmodel]
to illustrate estimation of tree density, species composition, and stand tables.

[^uav-data]: We thank Kai Jütte for initiating and supporting the Weisse Krug study.
    OGF GmbH acquired and provided the UAV laser scanning data used in the
    forestry examples on behalf of the State Forestry Agency of
    Mecklenburg–West Pomerania.

The magnitude, composition, DBH, and species-by-DBH articles use this same population.
The plot table contains the observations used for fitting. The prediction
table covers the forest and also contains simulated counts, giving us known
quantities against which to assess predictions.

::: {.alert .alert-info role="note"}

Extract it and use the folder containing `data/` as your R working directory.
The download includes the simulated counts, ready for fitting. The generation

## Forest, plots, and prediction cells

The forest comprises 249 stands. Its 151 field plots are circles of radius
20 m, clipped to the forest boundary where necessary. The prediction grid
contains 4,812 square cells, also clipped to the forest boundary. A full cell
has the area of a full plot, approximately 0.126 ha, and a side length of
35.45 m. At each plot and prediction cell, p95 is the 95th percentile of
canopy-height model values within its forested area, measured in meters.

We begin by reading the forest polygon and the plot and prediction tables.
We also calculate the forest area with `st_area()`, converting square meters
to hectares.

```{r}
#| label: read-data
```

The forest covers `r round(forest_area_ha, 1)` ha. The `area` column
in each table gives the forested area of that plot or cell in hectares.

We map p95 across the prediction cells and add the plot locations.

```{r}
#| label: fig-forest-map
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Canopy-height predictor p95 across the forest. White circles mark the 151 plot locations. The colored cells are the locations used for forest prediction."

prediction_cells <- st_read("data/prediction_cells.gpkg", quiet = TRUE) |>
  inner_join(prediction |> select(plot_id, p95), by = "plot_id")

plot_locations <- st_as_sf(plots, coords = c("easting", "northing"),
                           crs = st_crs(forest))

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = prediction_cells, aes(fill = p95), color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = forest, fill = NA, color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf(data = plot_locations, shape = 21, fill = "white", color = "black",
          size = 1.5, stroke = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "p95 (m)") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

Canopy height varies across the forest. We use it as a predictor in each
model component, with separate coefficients for overall density, species
allocation, and diameter allocation within species.

## Generate tree counts

### Standardize canopy height

We standardize p95 using the plots' mean and standard deviation, applying
those same values to the prediction cells. The resulting predictor `x`
has mean zero and standard deviation one among the plots. Centering makes
the intercept refer to average canopy height, and scaling expresses the
slope per one-standard-deviation increase. It can also help numerical
stability during fitting. We combine plots and prediction locations to
generate all counts together.

```{r}
#| label: scale-predictor
```

### Overall tree density

For a unit with forested area $a_i$ hectares, expected tree density $M_i$
and total count $N_i$ follow

$$
\log M_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i, \qquad
N_i \mid M_i,r_M \sim \operatorname{NB}(a_i M_i,r_M).
$$

The negative-binomial mean is $a_i M_i$, and $r_M$ is its size parameter.
For the simulated population, we set $\beta_0 = \log(350)$,
$\beta_1 = -0.2$, and $r_M = 50$. Expected density is therefore 350 trees/ha
at average plot p95. A one-standard-deviation increase in p95 multiplies
this density by $\exp(-0.2)$, about 0.82, an 18% decrease. We use these
parameter values to calculate expected densities and simulate counts at
all plot and prediction locations.

```{r}
#| label: magnitude
```

`expected_density` is the mean density specified by the model; `count` is
one simulated total count for that area. The realized density `count / area`
varies around the expected density. We plot the simulated plot densities
against p95, with the generating mean shown as a line.

```{r}
#| label: fig-plot-counts
#| fig-cap: "Simulated plot densities and their relationship with canopy height. The black line shows the generating expected density."

relationship <- tibble(p95 = seq(min(plots$p95), max(plots$p95), length.out = 100)) |>
  mutate(expected_density = exp(beta_0 + beta_1 * (p95 - p95_mean) / p95_sd))

locations |>
  filter(dataset == "plot") |>
  ggplot(aes(p95, count / area)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "#31688E") +
  geom_line(data = relationship, aes(y = expected_density), color = "black") +
  labs(x = "p95 canopy height (m)", y = "Trees per hectare") +
  theme_bw()
```

### Species allocation

We allocate the total among pine, oak, and birch using sequential probit
probabilities. Pine is allocated first. Oak is allocated among the trees
remaining after pine, and birch receives the rest. These binomial draws
together produce a multinomial allocation of the total count.


</details>

The positive pine slope increases its share as p95 increases. The negative
oak slope decreases its share of the trees remaining after pine. The three
species counts always sum to the total count at that location.

### DBH allocation within species

We next allocate each species' trees among five diameter-at-breast-height
(DBH) classes. Each class includes its lower boundary and excludes its upper
boundary; `50+` includes all diameters at least 50 cm. Thus, all simulated
trees have DBH of at least 10 cm.

Each species has its own intercepts and slopes. As with species allocation,
we draw counts for successive classes from the trees remaining, with the
largest class receiving the remainder.

<details>
<summary>DBH allocation code</summary>

```{r}
#| label: dbh
```

</details>

There are 15 species-by-DBH categories. Their counts sum to the total at
each location. There are no spatial or group effects, and the DBH-class
coefficients are specified directly without a smoothing model. Expected
densities and allocations vary with p95.

## Known forest quantities

We calculate forest density by averaging the simulated cell densities,
weighted by their areas. Boundary cells contribute less because they cover
less land. This gives a grid approximation to forest density in trees/ha.
Multiplying that density by the polygon's forest area gives the corresponding
forest total. The same calculation applies to each species-by-DBH category.

```{r}
#| label: forest-truth
```

The simulated forest density is **`r round(forest_density, 1)` trees/ha**,
corresponding to approximately **`r format(round(forest_total), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)`
trees** over the forest area. These reference quantities come from the
simulated counts, including their count variation.

We arrange the category densities as a stand table, with DBH classes in rows
and species in columns.

```{r}
#| label: forest-table

forest_table |>
  select(species, dbh_class, density) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = species, values_from = density) |>
  mutate(dbh_class = factor(dbh_class, levels = dbh_classes)) |>
  arrange(dbh_class) |>
  select(dbh_class, pine, oak, birch) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1, col.names = c("DBH class (cm)", "Pine", "Oak", "Birch"))
```

When fitting the models, we will repeat this aggregation for each joint
posterior predictive draw. Summaries of those aggregated draws provide
forest estimates and intervals that we can compare with these known values.

## Cell areas within stands

To summarize predictions for stands or other polygon areas of interest, we
pass the posterior predictive samples stored in the object returned by
`predict()` to `standSummary()`, which handles the area-weighted aggregation.

Because some prediction cells cross stand boundaries, we need the area of
each cell within each stand. Each cell has one set of density draws, but its
contribution to a stand depends on how much of the cell lies within that
stand. For example, a hypothetical 0.12-ha cell split between two stands
would have two rows in the area table.

| `prediction_id` | `stand_id` | `area_ha` |
|:--|:--|--:|
| 1 | A | 0.08 |
| 1 | B | 0.04 |

Both rows use the same density draw for cell 1. If that draw is 300 trees/ha,
the cell contributes $300 \times 0.08 = 24$ trees to stand A's total and
$300 \times 0.04 = 12$ trees to stand B's total. For each draw,
`standSummary()` adds the contributions from all cells overlapping a stand
and divides by their summed area to obtain stand density. Repeating this
calculation across draws gives a distribution from which we calculate the
stand estimate and interval. This treats density as constant within each
prediction cell.

We construct the area table for our forest by intersecting the cell and stand
polygons and calculating the intersection areas in hectares.

```{r}
#| label: read-stand-polygons

stands <- st_read("data/stands.gpkg", quiet = TRUE)

cells <- st_read("data/prediction_cells.gpkg", quiet = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: cell-stand-areas
```

The saved table has one row per cell–stand intersection. `prediction_id`
matches the cell's `plot_id` in the prediction table, `stand_id` identifies
the stand, and `area_ha` gives the area of that cell within that stand.
A cell crossing a boundary appears in more than one row. Cell 248, for
example, contributes to two stands.

```{r}
#| label: preview-stand-areas

cell_stand_areas |>
  filter(prediction_id == 248) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 4)
```

We save this table once and reuse it with `standSummary()` in the later
modeling articles.

## Shared data files

The data bundle contains:

| File | Contents |
|:--|:--|
| `forest.gpkg` | The forest polygon, used for mapping and forest area. |
| `plot_locations.gpkg` | The original plot centers, ready to use in maps. |
| `stands.gpkg` | The 249 stand boundaries, stand IDs, areas in hectares, and stratum labels for the later example. |
| `plots.csv` | The 151 plot locations, stand IDs, predictors, areas, and simulated counts. |
| `prediction.csv` | The 4,812 prediction locations, stand IDs, predictors, areas, and simulated counts. |
| `prediction_cells.gpkg` | The prediction-cell polygons, linked to `prediction.csv` by `plot_id`. |
| `cell_stand_areas.csv` | The area of each prediction cell within each stand, for later stand summaries. |

Both location tables and the prediction-cell polygons use numeric `plot_id`
identifiers. The overlap table calls the same cell IDs `prediction_id`.

The `stand_id` column links locations to stand polygons. Cells that cross
stand boundaries have a separate overlap area for each stand in
`cell_stand_areas.csv`, allowing their predicted densities to contribute to
each stand they cover.

Both CSVs contain total count `count` and 15 category-count columns, such as
`pine:10-20`. The magnitude example uses total counts. The composition example
sums DBH-class counts within species and conditions on the totals. The DBH
example sums over species within each diameter class; the species-by-DBH
model uses all 15 categories. Prediction-cell counts provide known values for
assessment and are excluded from fitting.

We inspect the first few plots, showing total counts and the 10--20 cm counts
for each species.

```{r}
#| label: preview-data

plots |>
  select(plot_id, area, p95, x, count, `pine:10-20`, `oak:10-20`, `birch:10-20`) |>
  head() |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

We next fit a [magnitude model](magnitude-plot-sampling.html) to estimate
forest and stand tree densities from the sampled plots.
